newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-FRITZ STROBL LEADS AUSTRIAN RAID ON VAL D'ISERE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-FRITZ STROBL LEADS AUSTRIAN RAID ON VAL D'ISERE.

text.p: Unheralded Fritz Strobl led the Austrian ski racers on a rout on Sunday when they took the top four places in the opening downhill of the World Cup season.

Strobl, who had made little impact in the World Cup previously and started wearing bib number 43, pushed better-known team mates Werner Franz, Patrick Ortlieb and Josef Strobl out of the spotlight to snatch his first victory on the circuit in one minute 51.61 seconds.

Downhill World Cup holder Luc Alphand, the winner here last year, had to settle for sixth this time behind Italian Kristian Ghedina in cold, dry and sunny conditions ideal to finally launch a downhill season which had been hampered by bad weather until Sunday.
Strobl, a tall, heavy skier, is not related to Josef Strobl who won the first of two Val d'Isere downhills in 1994.
In the second, the Austrians enjoyed another clean sweep of the top four places, led by Armin Assinger.

Josef Strobl had looked set for a win here on Saturday when he had the fastest time of the early starters before fog on the OK piste forced organisers to call a halt to the downhill after 17 racers had gone. The race was rescheduled for Sunday with all the skiers starting from scratch.

On Sunday, competition within the Austrian team proved the motivation for Fritz Strobl, who had mostly competed on the European Cup circuit until now and was the 16th skier to collect his debut victory at Val d'Isere.
"When I saw that three Austrians were in the lead, I
told myself I had a chance especially as I had been as fast as them in training," said the 24-year-old military policeman, who comes from the same Kaernten region as downhill legend Franz Klammer.
"But to win is a surprise and I hope there will be others," he added.
A super-G specialist, Strobl may have another chance to shine on Monday when the first super-giant of the season takes place here.
For Franz, who had two previous second places to his name, missing victory by 0.02 seconds on 1:51.63 was a real disappointment.
"It was one of the hardest days of my life emotionally. I was sure I had made it at last and then I lost. But I'm confident I'll win the next one in Val Gardena," he said.
The Italian resort is hosting two downhills next weekend, including one postponed from Whistler, Canada, where heavy snow prevented racing earlier this month.

World champion Ortlieb, noted for his devil-may-care attitude to skiing, won Olympic gold on the same mountain in 1992 -- though on a different piste -- and said his mind had been on accumulating World Cup points rather than winning the race.
"My main goal this season is to win the World Cup at last and maybe I did not give it all I had. I skied like an old man, thinking above all about finishing to score points," he said.
Switzerland, traditionally Austria's greatest rivals on the slopes, had a bad day without a single man in the top 10. Veteran William Besse was their highest finisher, in 11th place.
Alphand, who has taken the downhill crystal globe in the last two seasons, admitted it would be hard to keep this winter.
"I'm not the pace setter any more but I'm not far back, which is the good news. But I will have to work very hard to catch the Austrians," he said.
Norwegians were among the other skiers to be disappointed on Sunday. Overall World Cup holder Lasse Kjus, winner of last season's closing downhill, did not start. He has influenza and bronchitis.
Current overall World Cup leader Kjetil-Andre Aamodt nearly went off course and finished 43rd.
But the most unlucky of the 72 starters was American Olympic champion Tommy Moe, who was flagged down after Canadian Graydon Oldfield fell just before him.
Moe, who had clocked the fastest intermediate time, had to be content with 35th spot after his second run, during which he was distracted by a skier standing on the piste.
